entry: Italian-born American mobster. Born Salvatore Lucania in [[Sicily]], he began his criminal career in [[New York City]]'s Five Points Gang and helped develop the National Crime Syndicate. He is considered the father of the [[American Mafia|Italian-American Mafia]]: in 1931 he established the Commission after abolishing the title of *capo dei capi* (boss of bosses). He was convicted in 1936 of running a prostitution racket and sentenced to thirty to fifty years in prison. In 1946 his sentence was commuted, for his alleged wartime cooperation with U.S. naval intelligence, on condition that he be deported to Italy, where he died.

Roman poet and philosopher. Titus Lucretius Carus wrote *De rerum natura* (usually translated as *On the Nature of Things*), his only known work, a didactic poem setting out the ideas of Epicureanism, including its atomism and [[Cosmology|cosmology]]. Very little is known about his life. He was a friend or client of Gaius Memmius, to whom the poem is addressed. It had a considerable influence on the Augustan poets, including [[Virgil]] and [[Horace]]. It was almost lost during the [[Middle Ages]] and was rediscovered in 1417 in a monastery in Germany by Poggio Bracciolini. The poem played a role in the development of atomism, influencing Pierre Gassendi, and in Enlightenment-era efforts to construct a new Christian humanism.

American actress, producer, and artist. Liu had her breakthrough as the attorney Ling Woo in the Fox series *Ally McBeal* (1998–2002). She also starred in *Charlie's Angels* (2000) and Quentin Tarantino's *Kill Bill: Volume 1* (2003). She played Dr. Joan Watson in the CBS crime drama *Elementary* (2012–2019), a modern version of [[Sherlock Holmes]]. She voiced Master Viper in the first three *Kung Fu Panda* films. In 2019 she received a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame, and in 2025 she gained renewed critical attention for *Rosemead*.

Fossil hominin skeleton of the species *Australopithecus afarensis*. Comprising 40% of a female skeleton, it was found in 1974 at Hadar, Ethiopia, by Donald Johanson of the [[Cleveland]] Museum of Natural History. Living about 3.2 million years ago, it had a small skull like that of non-hominin [[Ape|apes]] and an upright, bipedal gait. Pamela Alderman named it after the song "Lucy in the Sky with Diamonds" by [[The Beatles|the Beatles]]. In 2024 scientists agreed that her species was not the earliest known member of the human family.

19th-century English movement of [[Textile|textile]] workers opposed to automated machinery. Protesting over pay, working conditions, and output quality, the Luddites, who called themselves followers of the legendary weaver Ned Ludd, often destroyed machines in organized raids. The movement began in [[Nottingham]] and spread to the North West and [[Yorkshire]] between 1811 and 1816. Mill owners shot protesters, and the Luddites were suppressed by legal and military force, including executions and penal transportation. The term is now used for those who oppose new technologies.

City (pop., 2011: 1,618,879) in [[Punjab, India|Punjab]] state, northern India. Ludhiana is a major industrial center referred to by the BBC as "India's Manchester," and it is the commercial capital of Punjab. It was founded in 1480 under the Lodi dynasty of the [[Delhi Sultanate]] and was originally named Lodi-ana, meaning "the town of the Lodis." Its Lodhi Fort, popularly known as Purana Qila, is the only surviving monument from the city's foundation. Under Mughal rule it became part of the Lahore Subah, and under British rule it became a military cantonment and a commercial center. Its industries include woolen hosiery, knitwear, and bicycles, and it manufactures over 50% of India's bicycles.

Austrian mathematician and theoretical physicist. His greatest achievements were the development of [[Statistical mechanics|statistical mechanics]] and the statistical explanation of the [[Second law of thermodynamics|second law of thermodynamics]]. In 1877 he provided the current definition of [[Entropy|entropy]], S = kB ln Ω, where Ω is the number of microstates whose energy equals the system's energy. Entropy is interpreted as a measure of a system's statistical disorder. [[Max Planck]] named the constant kB the [[Boltzmann constant]]. Boltzmann held professorships at Graz, Munich, Leipzig, and Vienna. In his final years he spent much effort defending his atomic theories against energetics, championed by [[Ernst Mach]] and Wilhelm Ostwald. Experimental work by Jean Perrin later supported his atomic theories.

German-American architect and interior designer. Commonly known as Mies, he is regarded as one of the pioneers of modern architecture. His buildings used industrial steel and plate glass to define interior spaces, and he is associated with the maxims "less is more" and "God is in the details." He was the last director of the [[Bauhaus]], the German school of modernist art, design, and architecture, which closed under political pressure from the Nazi regime. He emigrated to the United States in 1937 or 1938 and headed the architecture school at what is now the Illinois Institute of Technology. His American works include the skeletal-frame Lake Shore Drive Apartments, the bronze-clad Seagram Building, and the glass-walled Farnsworth House.

Austrian-born British philosopher. Born in [[Vienna]] into one of Europe's richest families, he studied at the [[University of Cambridge|University of Cambridge]] from 1911 to 1913 under [[Bertrand Russell]], and he interacted closely with [[John Maynard Keynes]]. His early work, the *Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus* (1921), held that by explaining the logic linking propositions to the world he had solved all philosophical problems. He taught at Cambridge from 1930 to 1947. His later work, published posthumously as *Philosophical Investigations* (1953), rejected many assumptions of the *Tractatus* and argued that the meaning of words is best understood as their use within a given language game. He served in the Austro-Hungarian Army in [[World War I]] and was decorated for his courage. His time as a primary school teacher in rural Austria in the 1920s was controversial because of his use of violent corporal punishment.

German aviation holding company. Its principal airline, Lufthansa German Airlines, is the flag carrier of [[Germany]] and a founding member of Star Alliance. The group also owns Austrian Airlines, [[Brussels|Brussels Airlines]], Eurowings, ITA Airways, and Swiss International Air Lines. Deutsche Lufthansa AG was founded as Luftag in [[Cologne]] in 1953 by former staff of Deutsche Luft Hansa, which had been liquidated in 1951 because of its association with the Nazi regime during [[World War II]]. Luftag acquired the Luft Hansa name in 1954. The airline's main hub is at [[Frankfurt|Frankfurt]] Airport.

Small one- or two-person sled ridden lying face up and feet first, and the Olympic sport that uses it. Lugers start seated, pushing off with handles at the start ramp, and steer by flexing the sled's runners with their calves or by shoulder pressure. Racing sleds weigh 21–25 kg for singles and 25–30 kg for doubles. Luge is the fastest of the three sliding sports; lugers can exceed 140 km/h, and Manuel Pfister reached 154 km/h on a track in Whistler, Canada, before the 2010 Winter Olympics. The sport is governed by the International Luge Federation (FIL), separate from the [[Bobsleigh|bobsleigh]] federation. Luge was first included in the [[Winter Olympic Games]] in 1964. Germany has won over 80 Olympic medals, including 38 golds.

Italian physician and physicist who studied animal electricity. In 1780, using a frog, he discovered that the muscles of dead frogs' legs twitched when struck by an electrical spark, an early study of bioelectricity. He taught anatomy at the [[University of Bologna]] for most of his career and published his main work, *De Viribus Electricitatis in Motu Musculari Commentarius* (1791), which argued for an intrinsic "animal electricity" and provoked controversy across Europe. [[Alessandro Volta]] disputed the conclusions, arguing that the contractions depended on the metal cable used to connect nerves and muscles. Volta coined the term "Galvanism" for a [[Direct current|direct current]] produced by chemical action. Galvani, reluctant to take part in the debate, let his nephew Giovanni Aldini defend the theory.

Italian dramatist, novelist, poet, and short-story writer. Born in Girgenti (now Agrigento), [[Sicily]], into a family with interests in the sulfur industry, he completed high school in [[Palermo]]. He was awarded the 1934 Nobel Prize in Literature "for his bold and ingenious revival of dramatic and scenic art." His works include novels, hundreds of short stories, and about 40 plays, some written in Sicilian. His plays, including *Six Characters in Search of an Author* (1921) and *Henry IV* (1922), explore [[Humorism|humorism]] (*umorismo*), a critical awareness of life's illusions and contradictions. His tragic farces are often seen as forerunners of the Theatre of the Absurd.

Spanish-Mexican filmmaker of surrealist and satirical films. Buñuel collaborated with [[Salvador Dalí]] on *Un Chien Andalou* (1929) and *L'Age d'Or* (1930), both regarded as masterpieces of [[Surrealism|surrealist]] cinema. From 1947 to 1960 he worked mainly in [[Mexico]], making melodramas such as *Los Olvidados* (1950). Later films satirized social conditions, and *Viridiana* (1961), which criticized the Francoist dictatorship, won the Palme d'Or at the 1961 [[Cannes Film Festival]]. *The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie* (1972) won the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film. He was nominated twice for the Nobel Prize in Literature, in 1968 and 1972. Seven of his films appear in Sight & Sound's 2012 critics' poll of the top 250 films of all time.

Uruguayan footballer and striker. Nicknamed "El Pistolero," he has scored over 600 career goals for club and country and is Uruguay's all-time leading goalscorer. In 2013–14 with Liverpool he equaled the Premier League record of 31 goals in a 38-game season. At [[Barcelona]] he formed the MSN attack with [[Lionel Messi]] and Neymar, and he became the first player to lead [[La Liga]] in goals and assists at the same time. He won the 2011 [[Copa América]] and represented Uruguay at four [[FIFA World Cup]] tournaments. In 2024 he joined Inter Miami.

Brazilian politician and former trade unionist; president of Brazil from 2003 and again since 2023. Born in [[Pernambuco]], he worked as a child and did not learn to read until he was 10. As a [[Trade union|trade unionist]] he led the ABC workers' strikes against Brazil's military government in 1978–80, and in 1980 he helped found the Workers' Party. He was a leader of the 1984 *Diretas Já* movement for direct elections. After unsuccessful presidential bids in 1989, 1994, and 1998, he won in 2002 and was reelected in 2006. His first presidency expanded social programs such as *Bolsa Família*, but was marked by the Mensalão vote-buying scandal. He was sentenced to prison in connection with [[Operation Car Wash]] in a controversial trial, and the Supreme Federal Court later annulled his convictions. He defeated the incumbent [[Jair Bolsonaro]] in 2022 and won a record-breaking fourth term in 2026.

Croatian footballer and central midfielder. Modrić captains the Croatian national team and has played in every major tournament Croatia has qualified for, including every [[UEFA European Championship]] from 2008 to 2024. He won the Golden Ball as the best player at the 2018 [[FIFA World Cup]], where Croatia finished second. In 2018 he also won the Ballon d'Or, the first award since 2007 to a player other than [[Lionel Messi]] or [[Cristiano Ronaldo]]. With Real Madrid he won six [[UEFA Champions League]] titles among 28 major trophies, and in 2025 he joined [[AC Milan]].

American actor and teen idol. He became one as Dylan McKay on Fox's *Beverly Hills, 90210*, a role he played from 1990 to 1995 and again from 1998 to 2000. He later played Fred Andrews on [[The CW]]'s *Riverdale*. His films include *Buffy the Vampire Slayer* (1992), *8 Seconds* (1994), and *The Fifth Element* (1997). His final feature film, *Once Upon a Time in Hollywood* (2019), earned him a Screen Actors Guild Award nomination. He died of a stroke.

Soothing song or piece of music sung or played to children, usually to help them sleep. Also called a cradle song, the lullaby has existed since ancient times and is found in many countries. Lullabies are often used to pass down cultural traditions and to develop communication skills. They tend to have simple, repetitive melodies with mostly consonant intervals and slow tempos, and they are usually in triple meter, giving them a rocking motion. Infants have shown a strong preference for unaccompanied lullabies. The word derives from the Middle English *lullen* ("to lull") and *by* ("near"), and was first recorded c. 1560.

Medical procedure in which a needle is inserted into the spinal canal, usually to collect cerebrospinal fluid for testing. Also called a spinal tap, it is typically performed under local anesthesia and yields fluid for biochemical, microbiological, and cytological analysis. Its chief diagnostic use is in suspected [[Meningitis|meningitis]], since no other reliable test can exclude it; it can also help diagnose subarachnoid hemorrhage and detect malignant cells in the cerebrospinal fluid. Drugs such as anesthetics and [[Chemotherapy|chemotherapy]] agents may be injected through it. Increased intracranial pressure is a contraindication, because brain matter may be compressed and pushed toward the spine. Post-dural-puncture headache is a common side effect when a small atraumatic needle is not used. The procedure was first introduced in 1891 by the German physician Heinrich Quincke.

Wood processed into uniform sizes, such as beams and planks, mainly for construction. Lumber is used for framing and finishing, including floors, wall panels, and [[Window|window]] frames, and rough lumber is the raw material for furniture-making. Most lumber is softwood from [[Conifer|coniferous]] species such as [[Pine|pine]], [[Fir|fir]], and [[Spruce|spruce]]; about 80% comes from softwood. In the United States and Canada, timber refers to unprocessed logs or standing trees. In 1420 the [[Portuguese Empire]] colonized [[Madeira]], where settlers cleared forest for crops and the felled trees were processed at sawmills and shipped to the mainland. In 1593 Cornelis Corneliszoon, a Dutch windmill owner, invented the first wind-powered sawmill, which made converting logs into planks thirty times faster.

SI unit of luminous flux, the perceived power of visible light emitted by a source. One lumen is one [[Candela|candela]] emitted over one steradian of [[Solid angle|solid angle]], so an isotropic one-candela source emits 4π lumens. Unlike radiant power, which includes non-visible [[Infrared|infrared]] radiation, luminous flux is weighted by the eye's sensitivity to each [[Wavelength|wavelength]]. One watt of light at 555 nm, where the eye is most efficient, equals 683 lumens. One lux is one lumen per square meter.

French [[Photography|photographic]] manufacturers and pioneering filmmakers. Auguste and Louis Lumière were best known for their Cinématographe, a three-in-one device that could record, copy, and project motion pictures, and for the short films they made between 1895 and 1905. They patented several processes, most notably film perforations, which advanced film through the camera and projector. The family moved to [[Lyon]] in 1870. Their screening of a single film, *Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory*, in Paris on March 22, 1895, was probably the first presentation of projected film. Their first paid public screening, on December 28, 1895, is traditionally regarded as the birth of [[Film|cinema]]. By 1905 the brothers had withdrawn from the film business, and they went on to develop the Lumière Autochrome, the first practical photographic color process.

Radiated electromagnetic energy emitted per unit time, synonymous with radiant power. In astronomy, luminosity is the total energy a [[Star|star]], [[Galaxy|galaxy]], or other object emits per unit time, measured in watts. It is intrinsic to the object, unlike apparent brightness, which depends on distance. The luminosity of the [[Sun]], L☉, is often used as a unit, and the IAU defined a nominal solar luminosity of 3.828 × 10²⁶ W. A star's luminosity can be determined from its size and effective temperature, but for most stars neither can be measured directly. Stars also radiate [[Neutrino|neutrinos]], which carry off about 2% of the Sun's energy.

Astronomical event in which the Moon passes through Earth's shadow. Lunar eclipses occur during eclipse season, when the Moon's orbit lies approximately in line with Earth and the Sun. Also called blood moons, they are visible from anywhere on the night side of Earth, unlike [[Solar eclipse|solar eclipses]], and often last an hour or longer. They are safe to watch without eye protection. When the Moon passes through the umbra, it appears orange or red, because sunlight reaching it passes through Earth's [[Atmosphere|atmosphere]], where [[Rayleigh scattering]] removes short-wavelength violet and blue light. Penumbral eclipses, in which the Moon lies only in the penumbra, cause a subtle dimming and make up approximately one-third of all lunar eclipses.
